Representative study: Pilcher, J. J., & Huffcutt, A. I. (1996). Effects of sleep deprivation on performance: A meta‑analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 112(2), 265‑277.
Main finding: Poor/short sleep predicts lower positive affect and higher negative affect the next day.

Representative study: Bolger, N., & Zuckerman, A. (1995). Daily stressors and mood: A longitudinal study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 68(5), 1015‑1025.
Main finding: Frequency and perceived severity of stressors are strong within‑person predictors of momentary negative mood.

Representative study: Reed, J., & Buck, S. (2009). The effect of regular aerobic exercise on positive‑affect and self‑esteem. Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology, 31(5), 607‑619.
Main finding: Even light‑to‑moderate activity on a given day is associated with higher positive affect later that day.

Representative study: Kuppens, P., & Verduyn, P. (2017). Personality processes in daily life: The role of affective reactivity. Journal of Personality, 85(5), 571‑585.
Main finding: More frequent positive social contacts predict higher positive mood; negative interactions predict spikes in negative mood.

Representative study: Keller, M. C., et al. (2005). Affective responses to daily weather: A longitudinal study. Environment and Behavior, 37(5), 657‑679.
Main finding: Higher sunlight exposure and moderate temperatures are linked to increased positive affect; extreme heat or precipitation relate to higher negative affect.

Representative study: Jacka, F. N., et al. (2010). Association of diet quality with mental health in a community sample. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 92(5), 1155‑1162.
Main finding: Higher intake of fruits/vegetables and omega‑3 fatty acids predicts better mood; high sugar/caffeine spikes are associated with greater mood volatility.

Representative study: Simons, J., et al. (2014). Daily alcohol use and mood: A within‑person analysis. Addiction, 109(9), 1495‑1504.
Main finding: Evening alcohol consumption predicts lower next‑day positive affect and higher next‑day negative affect.

Representative study: Bränström, R., & Kvillemo, P. (2011). The impact of mindfulness on daily affect. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 67(9), 945‑958.
Main finding: Even brief daily mindfulness sessions are linked to higher positive affect and reduced negative affect throughout the day.

Representative study: Kudielka, B. M., & Kirschbaum, C. (2005). Sex differences in HPA axis responses to stress. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 30(7), 673‑682.
Main finding: Elevated cortisol awakening response predicts higher negative affect; menstrual phase influences mood variability in women.

Representative study: Twenge, J. M., & Campbell, W. K. (2018). Associations between screen time and daily mood. Clinical Psychological Science, 6(1), 3‑17.
Main finding: Greater non‑work screen time, especially social media, correlates with lower positive affect and higher negative affect on the same day.

Representative study: Almeida, D. M., et al. (2002). Daily life events and affect: A longitudinal study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(5), 822‑837.
Main finding: Positive events boost same‑day positive affect; negative events increase same‑day negative affect and can have lagged effects.
